Nearly 100 Politicians Pledge to Reject "RSS-Linked" Funds. Hindu Americans Ask: Who Decides What That Means?

A new political pledge has opened a larger question for the Hindu-American community: when does scrutiny of an organization become a loyalty test for individual American citizens?

Read the story 5 min read · News

60-Second Catch-Up The big picture. In a minute.

See all updates →

Paris opens inquiry after BAPS delegation visit leads to reports of female staff being moved from posts. BAPS denies requesting any restrictions.

Survey of 2,000+ respondents: 66% of Indian-American voters lean Democratic ahead of the midterms. Cost of living is the top concern.
2 min read · Indian Express, Sep. 9 · Note: Indian-American ≠ Hindu-American
Why This Matters
Political scrutiny becomes different when the category being scrutinized is undefined
Opposition to violence is not in question. The civic problem is whether American citizens can be screened or stigmatized based on someone else's definition of who is "RSS-linked" — without transparent criteria, due process, or a standard any campaign is required to follow.
See the bigger picture →
What A4H Is Doing
A4H has put its position on the public record — and it is more precise than a simple endorsement or rejection
A4H issued a public statement supporting democracy, nonviolence, religious freedom and pluralism — while opposing ideological profiling of Hindu Americans and calling for transparent criteria before any "RSS-linked" designation is applied to individual donors or citizens.

Analysis · Religion & Politics

Religion is becoming an explicit campaign tool in 2026. That has consequences for every minority community — not just one.

Reuters reports that several candidates are deploying Muslim identity as a campaign issue in contested districts, including in Michigan. The pattern matters beyond any single race: when religious identity enters electoral messaging as a liability, the logic does not stop at one community's door.

Leadership · From the Chairman
Dr. Romesh Japra on what A4H is building — and why Rajneeti is how it gets built
At the inaugural Rajneeti Summit in Milpitas, Dr. Japra told delegates that Hindu Americans must move from contribution to participation — from the operating table and the boardroom to the campaign trail and the city council chamber. "If you are not at the table, you are on the menu." Rajneeti is the mechanism he has built to change that equation.
"From school boards to the Presidency — we are preparing to lead at every level."
Inside Rajneeti →
Community Service · Fremont, CA
At the Festival of Globe health fair, physicians and volunteers showed up for neighbors — not for a headline
Alongside A4H's August Silicon Valley events, physicians, nurses and volunteers staffed a community health fair in Fremont. The work was quiet and practical: screenings, consultations, community conversation. Civic identity, in this context, meant being useful to the people around you.
See the community →
Voices · Next Generation
"I didn't think policy was mine to shape. Rajneeti changed that."
Younger participants at the August summit described a common experience: years of civic disengagement, followed by a realization that the political conversations happening around them — about their communities, their values, their futures — were happening without them. A4H Times wants to hear from them.
"If Hindu Americans aren't in the room, our concerns become footnotes."

Ideas, Culture & Identity

Essay

Your karma bhoomi and your heritage: must a Hindu American choose between them?

When RSS chief Bhagwat told British Hindus last week that their loyalty belongs to their country of residence — not to India — he was making a claim Hindu Americans have been navigating for decades. Dharma does not demand assimilation. But it also does not counsel withdrawal from the civic life of the country in which you live. An original A4H Times essay on what it means to bring Hindu values into American public life without turning Hindu identity into a political loyalty test.

A4H Times Editorial · Original essay · 7 min read

Hindu, Hindutva, RSS, RSS-linked: what these terms mean — and why the distinctions matter in American politics
